title: Fermat's theorem on sums of two squares (OPEN in this ledger)
statement: Every prime p with p = 1 (mod 4) is a sum of two integer squares. NOT ESTABLISHED HERE. Three of the four ingredients are: the composition identity (F:int-brahmagupta-fibonacci), the congruence half of the descent (F:int-two-squares-descent-cross-terms) and the algebraic half of the descent (F:int-two-squares-descent-step); the fourth, the entry point, is Int.firstSupplementaryLawResidue -- for p = 2m+1 prime with m even, -1 IS a quadratic residue mod p, so p divides x^2 + 1 for some x and SOME multiple of p is a sum of two squares. What is missing is the ingredient that makes the descent terminate.

formal.statement: theorem Int.fermatTwoSquares : ((x0 : AxNat) -> ((x1 : And (AxNat.le (AxNat.succ (AxNat.succ AxNat.zero)) (AxNat.succ (AxNat.mul (AxNat.succ (AxNat.succ AxNat.zero)) x0))) (((x1 : AxNat) -> ((x2 : AxNat.dvd x1 (AxNat.succ (AxNat.mul (AxNat.succ (AxNat.succ AxNat.zero)) x0))) -> Or (Eq.{1} AxNat x1 (AxNat.succ AxNat.zero)) (Eq.{1} AxNat x1 (AxNat.succ (AxNat.mul (AxNat.succ (AxNat.succ AxNat.zero)) x0))))))) -> ((x2 : AxNat.Even x0) -> Int.IsSumOfTwoSquares (Int.ofNat (AxNat.succ (AxNat.mul (AxNat.succ (AxNat.succ AxNat.zero)) x0))))))

provenance.source: Fermat's theorem on sums of two squares (asserted 1640, proved by Euler in 1749 by infinite descent); this row records the measured remaining gap after the two-squares lane (W3-10, ADR-1633)

prior_art.what: the theorem and its first published proof by descent
prior_art.attribution: standard textbook attribution; this lane did not consult the primary sources

notes: THE SIZED OBSTRUCTION, re-measured 2026-09-05 by lane int-order-two-squares (ADR-1647) and stated as an outcome rather than a feeling. STILL OPEN. The ordering half is now BUILT and is no longer the obstruction: F:int-exists-centered-representative gives the bounded choice of representative, F:int-sq-le-sq-of-neg-le-of-le the two-sided square bound, F:int-sq-add-sq-lt-sq-of-bounds the strict decrease, and F:int-descent-multiplier-bounds packages both halves of the termination argument in the shape the descent consumes (from m > 0 and m*q = c*c + e*e with c, e in the band, conclude 0 <= q AND q < m). CORRECTION to the previous version of this note, which said 'shape_search finds no natAbs_le_iff, no mul_le_mul over Int and no sq_le_sq': two thirds of that was already false when it was written. Int.nat_abs_le_iff_mul_self_le landed 2026-09-01 in nat_abs_mirrors.rs and Int.mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left was already declared; a freshly built shape_search on 2026-09-05 (declarations=3236, positive control Int.descentStep FOUND) finds both. Only sq_le_sq was genuinely absent. WHAT REMAINS, in the order it has to be built, each item verified absent in-tree on 2026-09-05 rather than inherited from a handoff: (1) THE ENTRY POINT. Int.firstSupplementaryLawResidue gives x with x*x congruent to -1 mod p; modeq_to_dvd turns that into p dividing x*x + 1, so k*p = x*x + 1*1 for some k. Centering x first (F:int-exists-centered-representative at modulus p) and applying F:int-sq-add-sq-lt-sq-of-bounds with the second representative fixed at 1 gives x*x + 1 < p*p, hence k < p by Int.lt_of_mul_lt_mul_left; 0 < k by Int.pos_of_mul_pos_left. The band hypothesis for the constant 1 needs 1 + 1 <= p, which holds because p = 2m+1 with m EVEN and p prime forces m >= 2. Nothing here is blocked; it is unbuilt. The declaration two_squares.rs's module doc names as already existing, declare_exists_mul_isSumOfTwoSquares_of_residue, DOES NOT EXIST -- the name occurs exactly once in the file, inside that doc comment, and is not in declare_two_squares_all. (2) THE NEW MULTIPLIER'S FACTORISATION. From m*p = a*a + b*b and centered c, e congruent to a, b mod m, one needs m to divide c*c + e*e, i.e. a q with m*q = c*c + e*e, before F:int-descent-multiplier-bounds applies. The congruence is c*c + e*e congruent to a*a + b*b = m*p congruent to 0, which is Int.modEq_mul and Int.modEq_add plus Int.modulus_modEq_zero, all present. (3) q > 0, i.e. q NOT ZERO. If q = 0 then c*c + e*e = 0, so c = e = 0 by Int.eq_zero_of_sq_add_sq_eq_zero (landed here), so m divides both a and b, so m*m divides m*p, so m divides p; with 1 < m < p and p prime that is a contradiction. The Int-to-Nat divisibility transfer for the last step is Int.nat_abs_dvd_nat_abs_of_dvd, present. This is the largest remaining piece and is the one that consumes the PRIMALITY hypothesis -- every other step needs only 0 < m < p. (4) THE INDUCTION. Nat.strongInduction (ADR-1614) at a Prop motive, over motive n := 0 < ofNat n -> ofNat n < p -> (exists a b, (ofNat n)*p = a*a + b*b) -> IsSumOfTwoSquares p. Quantifying over ofNat n rather than over an Int m with natAbs m = n avoids a bridge hypothesis; m is recovered from Int.of_nat_nat_abs_of_nonneg. The base case m = 1 is p = a*a + b*b directly. None of (1)-(4) is blocked on a missing capability; all four are unbuilt work, and the ordering argument that WAS the blocker is done.
